title: Gateless Barrier, Case 47: Tou-shuai's Three Barriers
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to embark on an open-ended inquiry into their true nature, leaving no stone unturned in their exploration. This process involves questioning initial thoughts and ideas, trusting only in the journey of discovery, and cultivating a mindset of wonder, trust, and openness. By embracing this attitude, we can gradually uncover our true nature, rather than arriving at a fixed understanding, and find freedom from the constraints of life and death.

sentences.text: *And unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, it's the truth of the Tathagatas.*
Good evening everybody, good to see you.
Earlier I thought, wow, it's really getting dark out, and all your little squares are so dark.
Then I realized I'd turned the brightness way down on my screen, because I was running out of batteries earlier, so I was able to push a button and make you brighter again.
But we're still getting darker as we turn towards the winter, aren't we?
I just want to mention Dokusan again.
I'm more than happy to just sit, but you might as well put me to work.
It's good practice to meet for Dokusan, and also to see John and Edie and Chris, everyone else who's available to be seen.
It's not because we're desperate or need questions answered.
It's more like such a powerful ritual to do, kind of like co-regulating Zen, to do Zen as a ritual conversation.
It's a core practice, so come to Dokusan.
Judith and I took a little trip to Dublin, Ireland on Tuesday.
Just yesterday, we really got there quick and got home really easily.
It was no problem.
And it was nice.
They have a little different form, but basically all pretty familiar.
I gave a talk introducing the whole koan thing, so if you've been feeling a little bit bamboozled, maybe that talk will be helpful.
Ken's agreed to put it up on our website, a little introductory talk.
They turned out to be super serious about Dogen, especially the essays in Shobogenzo, because they're in the lineage of Nishijima Roshi, a Japanese teacher who worked with Westerners.
He and his English student, actually, Chodo Tom Cross, put out the first complete English translation of Shobogenzo.
Their group in Japan then, in the 70s and 80s, I think, was called Dogen Sangha.
Anyway, the Irish priest there, Myozan, made a vow to give a talk on every single fascicle in Shobogenzo.
I know.
I know.
I'm like, darn it.
I thought I was almost done with this kind of business.
So I'm going to have to go into Dogen next.
We'll see.
I can't imagine giving only one talk about most of those essays, though.
It seems like each one needs four or five talks, so I'll have to ask him how he does it.
But they haven't really studied koans, and several of them sent me little notes later saying, well, those feel more accessible to me now, and I was intimidated by koans.
Well, I wasn't hoping that they were intimidated by them, but I was hoping that I could help a little bit.
So that was nice.
So, speaking of koans, Mumonkan, Case 47.
*Tu Shuai, Great Master Tu Shuai, set up three barriers for his disciples.
One, leave no stone unturned to explore profundity.
Simply see into your true nature.
Now I want to ask you, just at this moment, what is your true nature?
Two, if you realize your true nature, you are free from life and death.
Tell me, when your eyesight deserts you at the last moment, how can you be free from life and death?
Three, when you set yourself free from life and death, you should know your ultimate destination.
So when the four elements separate, where will you go?*
Case 47 is like a little Dharma talk in which the master sets up three practices for his students.

After explaining, or giving at least the title of each practice, he challenges them, and he challenges us, to think about how we understand that now and to continue wondering how we will understand it as we keep practicing with it.
So here are his three barriers.
I mentioned the first one, you might remember vaguely, in Zazen, so I thought it was a good thing to practice with in Zazen.
*One, leave no stone unturned.
Explore the deep profundity.
Simply see into your true nature.*
And then he challenges us.
*Now I want to ask you, just at this moment, where is your true nature?*
Where did it go?
*Gate two, barrier two.
If you realize your true nature, how can you be free from life and death?
Tell me, he says, when your eyesight deserts you at the last moment, how can you be free from birth and death?
Three, when you set yourself free from life and death, you should know your ultimate destination.*
Destination.
Then he challenges us.
*So when the four elements separate, where will you go?*
Four elements being air, water, fire, and earth, all the components of the body.
So towards the end of the Mumonkan, we return to this fundamental theme of who and what we are.
Or maybe this has been the ongoing theme.
But here we explicitly hold up the mirror, the Zen mirror of birth and death, of life and death.
I was just seeing that a little more clearly: that mirror is held up as a way to really look at ourselves, really understand what this is.
It's not just palliative care planning or something like that.
It's a pointing or a mirroring of our true nature.
So what is our true nature?
I felt a great urge when I was preparing the talk to try to figure out the answer to that for you.
What does that mean?
What is your true nature?
What did that mean to these Chinese Chan masters?
What did it mean in terms of the broader Mahayana movement at the time?
I was hoping for some scholarly clues.
Or maybe I was hoping for a scholarly out.
So I actually looked up the Chinese characters that are being used for true nature, thinking maybe there's some cool etymology.
At least I could get a few interesting paragraphs out of it, if not a good useful pointer.
But not really.
The first character just means self.
The second character means the nature of a person, like one's destiny, one's disposition, one's nature.
So it really just means self-nature, true nature, self-nature.
So I looked to see what Nyogen Senzaki Roshi has to say about this case.
I just was feeling this urge.
Do you feel this urge?
Like, okay, what's the answer?
What do we do?
What is this true nature that we're supposed to look into, leaving no stone unturned and looking into the depths?
Here's what Senzaki Roshi said.
*All the koans in the gateless gate deal with one's true nature.
They begin with Joshu's mu, Gutei's finger, Suigan's inner master, the six patriarchs' true self, Bodhidharma's pacified mind.
Each leads the student directly to the region of Buddha nature.
Anyone who has experienced turning inwardly can actualize this, with ease, at any time.
It is not confined in a thing.
Therefore, it will be discovered in everything.
It is not excluded from a place.
Therefore, it will be exposed in every place.
The first barrier of Totsusu is, now, where is your true nature?
The moment of your hesitation, you are far away from it, 10,000 miles away.*
He's using there the Japanese voicings of the names of the masters we've studied over the years in this book.
But these are powerful pointers that he's offering.
And, of course, we shouldn't be surprised he's not offering some kind of answer.
How could he or anyone answer?
How could we answer this question of our true nature?
The koan gives us, first, a process, and then Senzaki Roshi gives us some direction.
The koan says, leave no stone unturned.
That's not just a throwaway line.
There never are any throwaway lines in this literature.
Keep exploring.
Keep wondering.
Keep looking.
Leave no stone unturned.
Don't trust your first ideas or your usual idea about who you are, who the others are, what anyone needs.
You've hardly turned over any stones yet, you know?
You're walking on top of them.
You can't even turn them over.
So do not be so convinced by our brilliant ideas, insights, intuitions, at least not at first.
It really is amazing the way the mind can fool us with its impressions, its simplifications, its projections.
We all want the answer.
That's the problem.
That's what obscures true nature, in a way: trying to figure out what true nature is is an obscuration of true nature.
It's not that kind of thinking or that kind of thing.

Sometimes when we have big life changes and crises and transitions, which we've all had and are all having, and I've been involved in that myself lately, maybe then we get a little shaken up in a way that occurs to us to look down and see that we're standing on these stones.
Maybe it's time to look under them.
Maybe it's time to look more closely at our ideas, our fears, our assumptions.
And it's not so easy, right?
There's a certain comfort to the way we always think that we are.
There's a certain comfort to our philosophy and our theories, even if we know in our heart of hearts that our theories and our philosophies often don't make us quite as happy as we might like.
So Suzuki Roshi says, this is a path, and you're never far from it.
You're never far from it.
It's an effort, it's an investigation, it's a life's work or many lifetimes' work.
But it's also easeful, it's also joyful.
As you get close to it, he says, as you turn inwardly to actualize it, you feel it with ease.
"Anyone who has experienced turning inwardly," said Suzuki Roshi, "can actualize this with ease at any time.
It's not confined in a thing."
So it will be discovered in everything.
It's not excluded from a place, so therefore it will be exposed at every place.
This turning inwardly to actualize it makes it sound like you could just one day turn the right way.
Maybe you can.
Maybe there are sudden shifts in this path, I think so.
But overall, it's more like a gradual rising of the light in the early morning.
What's great about the rising of the light in the early morning is you don't really have any doubt, right?
Even though it's really dark, maybe you're not too excited about being awake at this moment.
Maybe you had a bad night or a bad year, or you're confused about something.
But you don't hide back under the covers out of fear that the day will never come.
You don't wonder, I wonder if we'll be lucky enough to have a day today.
Gosh, I hope so.
We really need a day.
I really need growth.
I really need change.
I really need to wake up.
No, you have total faith, right?
You know that the light's going to gradually rise, and then it will be day.
I think it's like that with our practice.
We know that it's functioning.
We know that it's taking care of us.
We know that we have to make effort.
But we don't really have to have any doubt, because there's some ease to it, and it's not confined in a thing, and it's available in every place.
So I think it's really good to renew our contact with how wonderful the dawn is, and how beautiful the sunset is, because this is all mirrored in the world of life and death.
We've had friends and Sangha members pass away, and soon we'll have more, and in a flash of an eye, everyone in this Zoom call will not be in this world in the way that we are now.
And yet, we are part of this functioning, part of this turning of the wheel, too.
In our passing, we are also offering to the world ease and love, and an expression of our true nature.
Because, as it says, when you realize your true nature, you're free from life and death.
Even, as he says, very graphic in the koan, right?
At that moment, when things go black, your eyesight deserts you at the last moment before you stop breathing.
Will you feel your freedom?
Will you feel your freedom?
And will you know where you're going?
Everywhere, right?
You're going everywhere, and you'll be available and exposed at every place.
Because the Dharma Wheel, just like the Earth Wheel and the cycles of human society, will just keep turning.
And it's hard when we're on a downswing, or at least it appears like we might be on a downswing with some of these wheels.
But these teachings really encourage us so much, don't you think?
You can trust the wheel to come around.
It's natural.
It's organic.
We don't have to all jump up and down and get a big long rope to try to keep the Earth turning.
We trust the Earth to keep turning.
We trust our hearts to keep blossoming.
And we trust even the people that we are most confused by and most challenged by, that they, too, naturally will wake up.

Even in the chaotic room and all the chaotic households throughout our land last night, if you had anything to do with the debate, even the exhausted moderator, the shocked journalists ready to [unclear: "pund it away"].
I thought Wallace remained remarkably cheerful.
How did he do that?
He must be a deep practitioner.
He had a smile on his face at the end there, and he said, "That was something."
Didn't he say something like that?
So maybe he was somehow in touch with all this, even after such a challenging, what must have been the most challenging day on the job in his whole career.
So as Senzaki Roshi says, true nature is not confined.
It's everywhere.
It's everything.
Nothing is left out.
So this is a deeply generous and inclusive vision.
Why not have this be the true nature of all life?
And probably the Zen masters would not like this word "vision."
That sounds a little too narrow, like something you can see or not see, or a vision is something you think of that you never thought of before.
But nature has got to be bigger and broader and deeper than that.
So everywhere we go, we can be holding this question, this practice: leave no stone unturned.
What is this, this moment, this tree, this person, this breath, this confused political situation?
What is its true nature?
What is my true nature?
And maybe we can cultivate an assumption of abundance.
True nature is so rich, so wondrous.
Instead of investing in an assumption of poverty and loss, we get to choose our attitude.
So why not?
Who knows what's really true, or if there is such a thing as really true?
And how could any one thing be really true when it's all a giant cycle and it's all going around and around?
Maybe this great wheel has some bumps in it.
Whoa!
Maybe we're in a big bump on the wheel as it turns around, and it just hit the ground.
That's good.
That means it's going to head back up again soon.
But this teaching from Toushuai is not just an obscure Zen thing, I don't think.
It's life advice for all of us.
It's relationship advice, it's human advice.
Turn over the stones.
Look deeply.
Feel deeply.
Don't settle for appearances.
What's on the other side of that stone, of that idea, of that political persuasion?
What's on the other side?
And if this side looks dark, maybe the other side is light.
If this side looks full of hate, maybe the other side is full of love.
You won't know unless you do the work, right?
Unless we all do the work.
Unless we all continue to turn over stones and turn wheels and maintain the great functioning of this world, this universe.
It needs us.
It needs us.
One of my teacher friends has a great expression about curiosity.
She said so easily we fall into a kind of curiosity that, I don't know if she made this up or heard it from somebody, she called deficit curiosity.
That's the curiosity of not having enough, of things not being right, of wanting more.
That's the kind of greedy, short-attention-span curiosity: deficit curiosity.
So that's not the kind of curiosity we should use to turn over stones and look at the other side of things.
She suggested that there's another kind of curiosity called interest curiosity.
Maybe we can also have trust curiosity, where we're just deeply interested and trusting and wondering.
But there's no problem, there's no problem.
We just want to know what's over there, what's next.
Maybe it'll be something so surprising, so unexpected.
So this is an open-hearted practice, this way of being, this curiosity about true nature.
It's broad.
It's open.
It's all about not knowing, right, instead of all knowing.
Turning over the stones is releasing the idea that we already know what's on the other side.
We don't know.
We really don't know.
We don't know how the wheel will turn or where we'll end up.
We don't know what will happen as our sight fails and we breathe our last breath.
But we're curious.
We're looking forward to it, right?
What will that be like?
Senzaki, again, let's hear his pointers again.
I think they're so good.
*Anyone who has experienced turning inwardly can actualize the same with ease at any time.
It's not confined in a thing.
It will be discovered in everything.
It's not excluded from a place.
It will be exposed at every place.*
So just a deep bow to Senzaki Roshi for helping us, for leaving us that little roadmap.
And as Toushuai tells us at the very beginning, this seeing into our true nature is the first barrier.
It's the way.
It's the path.
And there's always more.
It's just the first of infinite barriers.
He mentions three, but really what he means is infinite barriers.
In "barrier," we think of barrier as a problem, and here barrier is not a problem.
Barrier is a beautiful opportunity.
Barrier is a practice.
Barrier here is a gift, a gift from the ancestors.
We're lucky they would give us that structure, give us that support, and not just leave us running around in circles with our heads cut off.
Wrong kind of running around in circles.
And the second barrier: if you realize your true nature, you're free from life and death.
So free from our fear of death, right?
Now we might understand this.
If we can feel our fluid, radiant nature, we really see how everything's changing all the time.
It's not just like we're cruising along alive and suddenly we're dead.
No.
Our life and death journey is always in motion, always changing.
Everyone we know and love who's alive also has this nature of dead, this nature of not alive.
We're here and we're not here, or we're not here in the way we think we are.
We make life so narrow out of our fear of death.
So having this freedom of life and death makes our life much bigger, right?
Much more possible.
So that's another implication of true nature, the way he's describing it.
It's like the great Tibetan Lojong practice, all those slogans.
My favorite one in there is seeing life as a dream.
So that's like this, right?
You don't need to make it into a narrow nightmare.
You can make it a big dream.
And this beautiful dream includes all of us passing away from this apparent form, even though the form we're in today is different from the form we were yesterday anyway.
We're already changing and transforming our form.
But there does seem to be a notable shift at that moment.
Which makes me think, of course, of Diane and Talus practicing all this so powerfully.

I don't know if you got to see it, but Talus at one point in that process, or after Diane had passed, sent out a video of himself rolling Diane's body on the gurney out of [unclear: "Wacom"] Hospice House.

And the staff all gathers around to thank him and to thank Diane for the privilege of being able to walk with them and walk over those last stones, turn over those last stones of Diane's life together.
It's only a two-minute video, but it just moved me to tears.
So beautiful.
Deep bodhisattva work.
And watching it, I learned a lot about this koan, I think.
And I learned a lot about life and death.
And Diane was a great teacher of life and death, don't you think, if you got to know her a little bit?
An elegant teacher.
Very elegant.
Showing how to live and showing how to die.
Wherever she is, I'm sure she feels our love and gratitude for her generous teachings.
Because, as it says at the very end of the case, the very end of Toushuai's teachings, when you set yourself free from life and death, you should know your ultimate destination.
I don't know how, but somehow Diane knew her ultimate destination.
And she could share that feeling with us, even if she couldn't leave a map.
That feeling of knowing.
That feeling of confidence.
That feeling of allowing the wheel of birth and death, the wheel of the earth, the wheel of our crazy society to turn.
So where are you going?
I'm really asking.
Where are you going?
It's a good question to feel into.
Not to try to figure it out or make your 10-year plan.
And some of us maybe don't have 10 years.
Maybe a lot of us, more than we know.
No.
Where you're going is about right now, this moment.
It's not about later.
What is your ultimate destination?
Also about right now.
So what's your intention, in other words?
How are you directing your life energies?
I had this image of each of us shooting out these strands of light.

And the light, we can send it out, but we can't really control it, because it bends according to all these other forces and everybody else's light and darkness and all the causes and effects and all the karma in the world.
But we courageously and confidently, as confident as we are of the rising of the day, of the light, we send out our light.
So where are you sending it?
So anyway, at least that's what came up for me, considering this case.
And even after we put this book down collectively, I hope you'll go back to some of these stories, any of these stories that really struck you, and really take them up in your own way.
It's good to read them with a friend, too.
I'm surprised how much more comes up if you're reading out loud with a friend.
You can have some Dharma dialogues and stuff.
Because this is a powerful literature.
It's a weird literature, no question.
But that's all right, we're weird.
It's sort of unyielding, in a way.

I was sharing with the group in Ireland that every time I've sat down to write one of these talks, so now almost 48 of them, and I did a bunch before that, too, so maybe 50, 60, 70 talks on koans, every single time, about a half hour into planning the talk, I would just hit this little wall.
I'd be, "Oh, no, this one's too hard.
I won't come up with anything to say about this.
This is a total flop.
It's going to be a five-minute Dharma talk.
I should find some long poem to read.
Maybe there's some more sweet stories in the New York Times."
I don't know if you noticed, but I did do that one night.
I wasn't up for it.
And yet, and yet, every time, so far, you stay with these stories, and these stories show you something.
They share something with you.
And I don't know if it's the story, the koan sharing something with you, or if it's the koan somehow catalyzing or allowing or making space for you to see something in yourself.
You didn't quite see it before that moment, but somehow, you were ready.
It was time.
These things happen in their own way, at their own pace, for sure.
But somehow our practice, which includes study and meditation and sangha life and dokusan, did I mention that before?

Somehow it's catalyzed and supported and enriched through the support of these [unclear: "quirkies"] and ancestors, even with all the problems of them being in another culture and another time, and all male, all misogynist and all that.
Sure, there's problems.
But would we turn down this beautiful world-turning gift just because it's not perfect?
That would be a little ungracious of us.
It would be ungenerous.
So we're lucky.
We're lucky we have so much support, every one of us, on so many levels.
We wouldn't be here without it.
